entries.clue: County put on bash with horse (7,5)

indicatorNotes.put on: To put one thing on another is to set it down against what is already there, so the two pieces are written as one unbroken run.

blocks.note: Suffolk is the East Anglian county on the North Sea coast, north of Essex
a bash is a blow struck with the fist, and so is a punch

annotation.surface: A county laying on a party, with a horse somewhere in attendance.
annotation.walkthrough: Bash is a party in the surface and a blow in the wordplay. The Suffolk Punch is Britain's oldest heavy draught breed, a stocky chestnut farm horse named for the county that made it.
annotation.definitionFit: The Suffolk Punch is a breed of heavy working horse, so the bare word 'horse' names the answer by the animal it is.

entries.clue: Dress unnecessarily concealed (4)

indicatorNotes.concealed: Something concealed is already sitting where it is hidden, so the letters are lifted unbroken out of the word beside it.

blocks.note: the run begins at the second S and crosses no space at all

annotation.surface: A frock hidden away for no good reason.
annotation.walkthrough: One long word holding a whole four-letter answer is harder to scan than a run across two words, because the eye takes it in as a single shape. A sari is worn wrapped rather than fastened.
annotation.definitionFit: A sari is the length of cloth an Indian woman drapes about herself and wears, which makes it a dress.

entries.clue: Soft soap, and what you put it on with? (7)

annotation.definition2: what you put it on with?

blocks.note: smarmy flattery or waffle, the talk used to butter somebody up

blocks.clueFragment: what you put it on with?
blocks.note: the small square cloth a British bathroom keeps by the basin, what Americans call a washcloth

annotation.surface: A mild bar of soap, and the thing you would lather it onto yourself with.
annotation.walkthrough: Soft soap is smarm, not a gentle bar, and the question mark admits the second half describes the answer rather than naming it. The two senses share a bathroom, which is what lets the sentence run on as one.
annotation.definitionFit: Flannel is British slang for waffling flattery, which is soft soap, and a flannel is also the cloth you soap yourself with.

entries.clue: Missing a brass band sound's great energy (5)

indicatorNotes.Missing: A thing that is missing is not there at all, so the letter named beside it is left out of what you write down.

blocks.note: the thumping bass figure a tuba plays under a brass band is an oompah
the single A dropped from the second syllable

annotation.surface: Take away a brass band's parping and the great energy goes with it.
annotation.walkthrough: The letter to drop is the indefinite article, which reads as ordinary grammar rather than as an instruction. The apostrophe-s is standing in for 'is' and joins the wordplay to the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Oomph is the word for drive and vigour — a car or a performance with oomph has great energy about it.

entries.clue: E-reader set alight (6)

blocks.note: Amazon's hand-held reading tablet, the device whose brand name became the word for the whole class
what a match and some paper do to a fire

annotation.surface: An electronic book gadget going up in flames.
annotation.walkthrough: Amazon named the device for the verb, the fire it starts standing for the reading it starts, so both halves of the clue are the same joke the marketing department made first. Three words, two meanings, no letters moved.
annotation.definitionFit: To kindle is to set a fire alight, and Amazon's Kindle is the e-reader that borrowed the word, so the trademark stands for the device.

entries.clue: At university, no two changes as yet (2,2,3)

indicatorNotes.changes: When something changes it does not stay as it was, so the letters beside it are set down in a different arrangement.

blocks.note: an Oxbridge student in residence is up, and down once term ends
five letters to be re-set

annotation.surface: On campus, not a single pair of alterations has happened so far.
annotation.walkthrough: Up for being at university is Oxbridge usage the crossword has kept — up for the term, down at the end of it, sent down for good if you misbehave. The comma after it hides the join.
annotation.definitionFit: Up to now means from the beginning of things until this moment, which is the job 'as yet' does in a sentence about what has not happened.

entries.clue: Furniture item caught on tresses (5)

indicatorNotes.on: One thing on another rests upon it, and in a down entry resting on something means being written above it.

blocks.note: c is how a cricket scorecard records a batsman out to a catch
tresses are long locks of hair

annotation.surface: A bit of furniture snagged on somebody's long hair.
annotation.walkthrough: Caught is the scorecard's c, written before the fielder's name when a catch ends an innings. 'On' is not idle here: it stacks the single letter above the word, which is the order a down entry reads.
annotation.definitionFit: A chair is the commonest single piece of furniture in any room, so the answer is named by the category it heads.

entries.clue: One falling for plumbing tool (7)

blocks.note: the agent noun from plunge: a person or thing that drops steeply
the rubber cup on a stick that a blocked sink gets worked with

annotation.surface: Somebody smitten with a plumber's gadget.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Falling for' reads as being infatuated, and the split runs between the two words instead: one who falls, then the tool. A plunger is also the gambler who stakes the lot on one bet.
annotation.definitionFit: A plunger plunges — dives or drops steeply — and a plunger is also the rubber cup on a handle used to clear a blocked drain.

entries.clue: Again take up weapons behind male (5)

blocks.note: somebody's behind is their rear
m is the standard mark on a form offering male or female

annotation.surface: Picking up arms once more from a position behind a man.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Behind' looks like the positional word telling you where the male goes, and it is a noun meaning backside. The definition runs to four words at the head of the clue, which is why the wordplay looks far too short.
annotation.definitionFit: To rearm is to take up weapons again, said of a country restocking its forces or of a fighter picking a gun back up.

entries.clue: Lab lent out for a game (7)

indicatorNotes.out: Something let out of its usual place no longer sits where it did, so the letters are written in another order.

blocks.note: seven letters to be re-set

annotation.surface: A laboratory loaned out to somebody for the afternoon.
annotation.walkthrough: Lab reads as a laboratory, a retriever or a political party, and is never more than three letters to shuffle. Netball is the seven-a-side court game played in British schools, descended from the earliest women's basketball.
annotation.definitionFit: Netball is a seven-a-side shooting game played on a court across Britain and the Commonwealth, so 'a game' names it by its category.

entries.clue: Where Paula Radcliffe was found, eventually (2,3,4,3)

blocks.note: reads as a question about tracking down a missing woman, and means the race she is in the middle of — Paula Radcliffe is the British marathon runner who held the women's world record for sixteen years
the flat everyday sense of the same phrase: after enough time has gone by for things to settle

annotation.surface: Somebody finally catching up with the missing marathon runner.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma before 'eventually' looks like part of the sentence about finding her, and it is the seam between the joke and the definition. A long run is where a marathon runner always is whenever anyone goes looking.
annotation.definitionFit: In the long run means once enough time has passed for everything to come out as it will, which is what 'eventually' says plainly.

entries.clue: Possesses a sleigh and is harassed (7)

blocks.note: one who possesses a thing has it
a sleigh is a sled, the runner-mounted sort you drag across snow

annotation.surface: A man who owns a sleigh and gets pestered about it.
annotation.walkthrough: The join falls in the middle of a double S, so the two pieces do not look like two pieces. Sleigh and sled name the same vehicle, and the grid wants the shorter of the two words.
annotation.definitionFit: To be hassled is to be pestered and pushed about by somebody, which is what being harassed means in everyday British use.

entries.clue: Even band claim best unscripted remarks (2-4)

indicatorNotes.Even: The even ones are the second, fourth, sixth and so on, so only every other letter of the run gets written down.

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth, tenth and twelfth of the thirteen letters, read straight through both spaces

annotation.surface: Even the band themselves reckon they are the best there is.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Even' is the instruction and also the grudging little word that makes the surface sound sour. Three words have to be read as one run of thirteen letters with both spaces ignored.
annotation.definitionFit: An ad-lib is a line a performer makes up on the spot instead of reading it, so ad-libs are remarks that were never scripted.

entries.clue: Where washer sat with city vessel (7)

blocks.note: Bath is the Somerset city built round the hot springs the Romans bathed in
a tub is a vessel, the open round sort

annotation.surface: The spot where a plumber's washer ended up, next to a boat out of the city.
annotation.walkthrough: A washer here is the person doing the washing, not the rubber ring inside a tap, and the definition is the whole opening phrase. The city is the spa town whose Roman baths gave it its name.
annotation.definitionFit: A bathtub is where a person washing themselves sits down, so the phrase names the answer by what goes on inside it.

entries.clue: Wrap with belt (6)

blocks.note: to wind cloth round something until it is covered over
a broad band or strip of country, as in a green belt or a belt of rain

annotation.surface: Bundling something up and strapping a belt round the outside.
annotation.walkthrough: Belt is the thing round your waist on the surface and a broad strip of country in the answer — a belt of woodland across a hillside. Both halves are one word each, and 'with' is the only other word in the clue.
annotation.definitionFit: To swathe is to wrap something round in cloth, and a swathe is also a broad band or strip of ground, which is one sense of belt.

entries.clue: Over the top royal award with outside contact (3,4)

indicatorNotes.outside: Whatever is outside a thing wraps round it, so the word named first is written round the letters that follow.

blocks.note: contact between two things is touch, and the word parts after its second letter to take what goes inside
the Order of Merit is the honour the British monarch hands out personally, limited to twenty-four living holders

annotation.surface: An honour from the palace, arranged with help from a contact outside.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Outside contact' reads as somebody beyond the circle putting a word in, and it is the instruction to wrap one word round the other. The Order of Merit is in the sovereign's own gift rather than the government's.
annotation.definitionFit: Something too much is more than anyone can be expected to stand, which is what going over the top amounts to.

entries.clue: Ring following trouble with reset music system (6)

indicatorNotes.following: What follows something comes along after it, so the single letter goes at the end rather than the front.
indicatorNotes.trouble: To trouble a thing is to disturb it, and letters disturbed do not stay in the order they were printed in.

blocks.note: five letters to be re-set
a ring drawn on paper is the letter o

annotation.surface: A phone going off just after some bother with a factory reset.
annotation.walkthrough: Ring stands at the head of the clue and its letter belongs at the tail, which is the whole job of 'following'. Trouble sits where a solver reads it as the noun in the sentence and is the verb telling you to disturb the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A stereo is the hi-fi that plays through two speakers, the ordinary household word for a music system.

entries.clue: New suit button is replacement (12)

indicatorNotes.New: Something new is not how it was before, so the letters after it are put together in a fresh arrangement.

blocks.note: twelve letters to be re-set

annotation.surface: A fresh button for a suit, handed over in place of the old one.
annotation.walkthrough: The fodder runs straight into the definition with nothing joining them, so the whole thing reads as one flat statement about tailoring. 'Is' looks like the verb holding the sentence up and is two of the twelve letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A substitution is the act of putting one thing in the place of another, which is what happens when a replacement is made.

entries.clue: Scuffle turning up in civil war battle (5)

indicatorNotes.turning up: Turning something up stands it on its head, and in a down entry that means the run is read from the bottom back to the top.
indicatorNotes.in: What is in something is already sitting inside it, so the letters are a run taken unbroken out of the words that follow.

blocks.note: the run LWARB begins at the last letter of CIVIL, takes all of WAR and the B of BATTLE, and is then read backwards

annotation.surface: A scrap breaking out at a re-enactment of a civil war battle.
annotation.walkthrough: A hidden run that reverses as well is out of sight twice over, and 'civil war battle' is so plainly a thing that nobody reads it as a row of letters. The entry goes down the grid, which is what makes 'up' a reversal.
annotation.definitionFit: A brawl is a rough, disorderly fight, which is what a scuffle turns into once it gets going.

entries.clue: A test involved a small sample only (5)

indicatorNotes.involved: Something involved is tangled up rather than laid out straight, so the letters come out in a tangled order.

blocks.note: five letters to be re-set

annotation.surface: A trial that needed no more than a tiny quantity to work with.
annotation.walkthrough: The opening 'A' is fodder rather than an article, which is the hardest habit to break in short anagrams. 'Involved' means tangled here, not concerned in something.
annotation.definitionFit: A taste of something is the little bit you are given to try — a mouthful and no more — so it is a sample of the smallest size.

entries.clue: Pole to practise boxing (4)

blocks.note: the stout timber a ship carries its sails and rigging on
what two fighters do in the gym, trading light punches neither is trying to land

annotation.surface: A length of timber set up for boxing practice.
annotation.walkthrough: Pole opens the clue, so its capital says nothing about whether the man from Warsaw is meant; the pole wanted is a mast or a boom. Two fighters sparring are rehearsing rather than fighting.
annotation.definitionFit: A spar is the mast or boom a ship hangs its sails from, which is a pole, and to spar is to trade practice punches in the ring.

entries.clue: Old thespian is a demanding person (7)

blocks.note: an ex-anything is the old one, as in an ex-wife or an ex-minister
a thespian is an actor, the name taken from Thespis of ancient Athens

annotation.surface: An actor past his prime who expects a great deal of everybody round him.
annotation.walkthrough: An exactor is one who exacts — extracts payment or obedience by pressure rather than asking — and the word is rare outside crosswords. 'Old' is the crossword's ex, saying nothing about anybody's age.
annotation.definitionFit: An exactor is somebody who exacts things from people, demanding money or obedience as a due rather than requesting it.

entries.clue: Sudden decline of small piece (5)

blocks.note: s is the size marked on a small garment's label
a lump is a piece broken off something bigger

annotation.surface: A sharp drop in the worth of one little chunk of something.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Of' joins the definition to the wordplay and hands over nothing, which is easy to miss while it reads as a genuine possessive. A slump belongs to the stock market and to a tired body equally.
annotation.definitionFit: A slump is a steep drop — in prices, in a player's form, or in somebody's posture — and so it is a sudden decline.

entries.clue: Stick as one to pool resources (4,8)

blocks.note: a club is the heavy stick a person hits with
people acting as one are acting together

annotation.surface: An instruction to stay united so that everybody's money goes into one pot.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stick' reads as staying loyal and is the blunt weapon instead. Clubbing together is what a British office does when it buys one leaving present rather than twenty small ones.
annotation.definitionFit: To club together is for several people to put their money in jointly so one thing can be bought, which is pooling resources.
